newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: MANDELA AIDE SEEKS RESPONSIBLE FINANCIAL MARKETS.
newsitem.headline: MANDELA AIDE SEEKS RESPONSIBLE FINANCIAL MARKETS.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela's chief of staff has called for global rules to protect developing countries from "the volatile unaccountability of the financial markets".

Gerwel, director general in the office of the president, made his call for greater fiscal responsibility in an address to the board of the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance (IDEA).
The text of Gerwel's speech was released on Tuesday after a two-day meeting of the board, which is chaired by former Commonwealth secretary general Sonny Ramphal.
Gerwel said a challenge to the concept of global governance, which IDEA seeks to promote, could be to "bring some global regularity to the world of international finance".
He said there was increasing adherence around the world to democracy, accountability and good governance, but no control on financial institutions and speculators.
South Africa had made every effort since the advent of democracy in April 1994 to establish responsible government, but remained vulnerable to financial speculators.
"The world and the developing world in particular seem to be at the total mercy of the ungovernable phenomenon of the international financial market.

"One observes how the volatile unaccountability of the financial markets expresses itself seemingly in total disregard for the relevance of the government's punctilious adherence to democratic and accountable governance as well as sound fiscal policy, he said.

South Africa has failed in the first two years of democracy to attract large-scale foreign capital investment and the rand currency has been battered by speculation since false rumours that Mandela was ill triggered a slide in February.

Finance Minister Trevor Manuel and Deputy President Thabo Mbeki, who is likely to succeed Mandela in 1999, have both condemned the superficial judgment of financial markets, which they have called amorphous.
Gerwel warned the Stockholm-based institute's leaders that concern for democracy in developing countries had to be matched by a commitment to social rehabilitation.
"Penury is an enemy of democracy in the long run and democrats and democratic forces will have to redouble their efforts to couple the spread of democracy with socio-economic development," he said.
Gerwel told Reuters later his remarks did not formally reflect government thinking or Mandela's personal concerns.
"I am asking, as a layman, is there anything that a government can do to be protected, or is that volatility totally beyond influence by a government's own exemplary behaviour," he said.
Gerwel said South Africa was given no credit for implementing a macro-economic strategy hailed by business and the International Monetary Fund as a model of fiscal responsibility.
